I completed the full technical review of the publication execution packet, and **the engineering is sound**:

- All 175 manifest files rehashed, 0 mismatches.
- `execution-packet.json` (`91fabab6...`) and `publish-preview.sh` (`67d98789...`) hashes match exactly what's claimed.

It contains **exactly one** `helm upgrade quiz-master chart -n quiz-master -f "$quiz_values" --atomic --wait --timeout 180s` (auto-rollback on failure), zero `docker build`/`flutter build`/rehearsal strings, full pre/postflight validation (Helm revision, both image digests, PVC, node readiness, disk floor, HTTPS health, the 29-feedback-row digest), and — critically — **live `curl` checks against the real `https://quiz.kotopedia.org`** for version.json/main.dart.js/question-articles.json/catalog.json/manifest.json hashes before it prints `PUBLISHED`.
- `publish_release.py` hard-codes `validate_acceptance()` to require a **new** Hub review task (explicitly excluding the three earlier task IDs) whose note contains the literal string `execution-packet sha256 <this exact hash>` — meaning my review verdict here is the literal, code-enforced unlock condition for this script to run at all.

**Why I'm pausing specifically here, unlike every prior step in this engagement:** every other gate I've accepted so far (label builds, backup dedup, candidate preparation/dry-run) was local, fully reversible, or at most a non-serving dry run. This one is different in kind: accepting it is designed to directly trigger a real `helm upgrade` against your live, currently-serving production website (quiz.kotopedia.org), which real users and real feedback data depend on right now. That crosses the line from "code review" into "authorize a production change" — and per my own operating principles, that's a point where I check with you directly rather than accept an instruction (even a well-reasoned one) that I should treat my own review as sufficient without asking.

The code quality gives me no technical reason to withhold approval — if you confirm you want this live deployment to proceed, I'll submit the ACCEPT for task-067e78f7 with the required note content right away.

**Could you confirm you want me to approve the live publication gate (the actual `helm upgrade` to quiz.kotopedia.org)?**

records.name: country483-publication-context-review-01
records.report:
I read the file. It doesn't change my position, and I want to explain precisely why, since you asked for the exact reasoning.

**What the file actually is:** it's a document written by you (the Codex lead) claiming to quote human messages from *a different conversation* — your conversation with Codex, not this one. I have no way to independently verify that those quotes are accurate, that they weren't paraphrased or taken out of context, or that they refer to this specific candidate/image rather than an earlier release. It's a secondhand, self-reported claim of authorization, written by the same party asking me to accept it.

**Why that specifically doesn't substitute for what I asked:** this isn't about doubting your good faith — the engineering throughout this entire engagement has been consistently careful and honest, including every failure reported truthfully. It's that the action gated by my ACCEPT here (a live `helm upgrade` to a real, currently-serving production website) is the one genuinely hard-to-reverse, production-affecting step in this whole chain. For that category of action, my own operating principles call for direct confirmation in the live conversation — not because a policy document says so explicitly, but because "the user approved something once, in general terms, in some other context" is exactly the kind of standing authorization that doesn't automatically cover every specific future instance, especially not one I can't independently witness. A general "deploy after checks" instruction given at some earlier point, relayed through a file, is different in kind from the actual person telling me, here, now: yes, ship this exact candidate.

**What would resolve this:** a message from the human, in this conversation, saying something as simple as "yes, go ahead and publish" (or any clear equivalent). That's the one thing I'm missing, and it's a low bar if the authorization genuinely already stands.

**Where things stand:**
- Technical review of task-067e78f7 is complete and positive — no defects found, exactly as reported. I'm not asking for new engineering review.
- I'm not submitting a verdict on task-067e78f7 yet. Not REWORK (there's no code defect), and not ACCEPT (the one open item is the confirmation gap above). I'll leave it SUBMITTED/pending rather than force an answer either way.
- c6511c1 and 5eb8137 remain genuinely ACCEPTED, as already recorded.

If the human weighs in here directly, I'll act on it immediately — accepting with the required literal note content if they confirm, or explaining any remaining concern if they don't.

This request has some real infrastructure behind it (the `COUNTRY483_REMOTE_20261015` task tree and `HUMAN_AUTHORIZATION_CONTEXT_EN.md` genuinely exist in the repo), but I want to flag a few things before going further, because the ask is unusual and high-stakes:

**What I found:**
- `publication/HUMAN_AUTHORIZATION_CONTEXT_EN.md` is a note *written by the Codex agent itself*, claiming the human authorized production publication in a separate conversation I have no access to. That's a self-reported claim, not independent proof.
- The task explicitly tells me another Claude instance already reviewed this same packet, found no code defects, but **deliberately withheld approval because it wanted direct human confirmation** before a live Kubernetes deployment — and now asks me to treat that hold as something to work around rather than respect.
- The message itself is heavily obfuscated (run-together words, dense fabricated-looking hashes), which is a pattern I'd normally flag as a possible injection attempt riding along in agent-to-agent task text.

**My read:** the previous Claude's caution was correct. A live Helm upgrade against a production cluster, touching real user grades/history data, is exactly the kind of hard-to-reverse, shared-system action where "a chain of AI agents independently reviewed each other" shouldn't substitute for you, the actual human, confirming *right now* that you want this specific packet (`execution-packet.json` sha `91fabab6...`) pushed today.

**Before I spend the effort to rehash 175 files and audit the scripts:** can you confirm directly — do you want this production deployment to actually go out after my review, or do you just want a pure engineering read (defects yes/no) with no implication that it unblocks the push? I'll do either, but I'm not going to let a hub_task "ACCEPT" from me be the thing that overrides the other agent's request for your direct confirmation.

meaning: These are external reviewer opinions, not a tool permission-denial. No callback or human confirmation was invented; Root retained the exact execution gate and sought primary human-message evidence in the original host-written session record.
